whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Claude Certified Architect Foundations exam for?

personas.label: Platform Engineers
personas.description: Engineers who design multi-agent systems, configure MCP servers, and build the infrastructure that other developers ship Claude-powered features on top of.

personas.label: DevOps and Infrastructure Leads
personas.description: Team leads responsible for integrating Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines, managing CLAUDE.md configuration hierarchies, and enforcing quality gates on AI-generated code changes.

personas.label: Senior Developers Moving Into Architecture
personas.description: Experienced developers who have built Claude integrations and now need to prove they can design reliable, multi-agent workflows with proper orchestration, failure handling, and context management.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Claude Certified Architect Foundations Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The CCAR-F is a significant step up from the Developer exam. It tests system-design judgment, decomposing problems into agent workflows, choosing MCP transport protocols, configuring Claude Code for team-wide consistency, and designing prompt architectures that stay reliable under production load. Candidates who have designed and operated a real multi-agent system find the exam manageable; those with only single-agent or prototype experience will find the orchestration and reliability domains challenging.
bullets: 720/1000 passing score: you must perform well across all five domains, especially the heavily weighted Agentic Architecture section.

Hands-on system design experience is essential: candidates who have built an MCP server, configured Claude Code at the team level, and debugged a multi-agent failure loop report the exam aligns closely with real-world problems.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: If you can design a multi-agent workflow, explain when to use stdio vs. SSE transport for MCP, and write a CLAUDE.md hierarchy that resolves cleanly, you are ready to book.

examFormat.heading: Claude Certified Architect Foundations Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online. Here is the format:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Almost every question describes a production system with specific constraints, latency requirements, compliance needs, team structure, failure modes, and asks which architectural decision best addresses the scenario. The exam tests tradeoff reasoning, not implementation syntax.
bestWayToPass: Build a multi-agent workflow end-to-end: Implement a coordinator that delegates to subagents, pass context between them, handle failures, and monitor the pipeline, this directly maps to the exam’s largest domain.
Stand up an MCP server with real tools: Expose a database lookup and a file reader, connect them to Claude Code, and debug tool-selection errors by refining your schemas.

Configure Claude Code on a real codebase: Write CLAUDE.md files at different directory levels, create custom slash commands, and set up hooks, the exam tests the configuration hierarchy and conflict-resolution rules.

Study failure modes, not just happy paths: What happens when a tool call fails mid-pipeline, when the context window fills up, or when an agent loops indefinitely? Catalog these scenarios and write recovery strategies for each.

keyConcepts.h2: Claude Certified Architect Foundations: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Designing Multi-Agent Systems
blocks.body: You need to decide when a single agent with several tools is enough and when to split work across specialized subagents coordinated by a hub.

blocks.heading: MCP Servers and Tool Boundaries
blocks.body: The Model Context Protocol gives Claude a standardized way to reach databases, APIs, file systems, and other services. split across two, when to use stdio transport (local, single-client) vs. SSE (remote, multi-client), how to write tool schemas tight enough that Claude rarely mis-invokes them, and what security controls to put between the model and your production systems.

blocks.heading: Claude Code for Teams and CI/CD
blocks.body: Claude Code is a terminal-based coding agent. You need to understand how CLAUDE.md files layer, user-level defaults, repo-root project context, directory-level overrides, and how to write custom slash commands, set permission hooks, and plug Claude Code into continuous integration pipelines so it can review pull requests, run migrations, or enforce style guides automatically.

blocks.heading: Prompt Architecture for Complex Applications
blocks.body: At the architect level, prompts are system components, not one-off instructions. You need to know how to enforce JSON output via tool-use schemas, build few-shot examples that handle edge cases, and design validation-and-retry loops that feed parsing errors back to Claude so it self-corrects. Expect questions on context-window budgeting, how much of the window to reserve for instructions vs. user content vs. tool results.

blocks.heading: Keeping Systems Reliable as They Scale
blocks.body: The final domain covers what goes wrong when an agent runs in production. You need iteration limits that stop runaway loops, circuit breakers that pause work and escalate rather than silently failing, context-management strategies for conversations that approach the window limit, and handoff patterns that pass curated summaries between agents instead of dumping entire histories.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Claude Certified Architect Foundations Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The CCAR-F rewards system-design instinct more than memorized syntax. If you have designed and operated a production system that uses Claude agents, MCP, or Claude Code at the team level, you are well-positioned. If not, build one first.

blocks.heading: Build a Multi-Agent Workflow End-to-End
blocks.body: Pick a task that naturally decomposes, say, research a topic, draft a report, and fact-check the result, and implement it with a coordinator agent that delegates to subagents. Pay attention to how you pass context between agents, where failures happen, and what metrics you would monitor. That experience directly maps to exam questions.

blocks.heading: Stand Up an MCP Server
blocks.body: Build a server that exposes two or three tools (a database lookup, a file reader, a webhook sender). Connect it to Claude Code or a custom agent. Notice when Claude mis-selects a tool and ask yourself what you would change in the schema to fix it. That debugging habit is what the MCP questions test.

blocks.heading: Configure Claude Code on a Real Codebase
blocks.body: Write CLAUDE.md files at different directory levels and observe how Claude Code merges them. Create a custom slash command, set up a pre-commit hook, and run Claude Code in a CI job. The exam tests the configuration hierarchy and conflict-resolution rules, hands-on experience makes those questions obvious.

blocks.heading: Practice Architectural Tradeoff Conversations
blocks.body: The exam is not about right vs. wrong; it is about better vs. worse given constraints. When you see a question with four plausible answers, ask yourself which option handles the constraint the question emphasized (latency? cost? security? compliance?) without introducing a new failure mode. That lens resolves most ambiguous choices.

blocks.heading: Study Failure Modes, Not Just Happy Paths
blocks.body: What happens when the third tool call in a five-step pipeline fails? What if the model hallucinates a tool name that doesn’t exist? What if the context window fills up mid-conversation? The exam loves these edge cases. Catalog five or six failure scenarios and write down the recovery strategy for each.

sampleQuestions.question: A legal team needs an agent that reads contracts, flags risky clauses and drafts revisions. Which orchestration fits best?
options: A single agent looped over the contract until it stops producing changes
Three agents working independently on the same contract and merging their output
A coordinator delegating each stage to a subagent
One agent that reads, flags and rewrites the whole contract in a single prompt
sampleQuestions.explanation: Separating extraction, risk assessment and drafting keeps each subagent's job narrow and auditable. A legal revision also needs human review before it counts as final.
whyWrong: Looping until the output stabilises is not a termination condition you can reason about for legal text.
Independent agents with no coordinator duplicate work and give you no defined merge semantics.
A single prompt covering all three tasks makes failures hard to isolate and the reasoning hard to audit.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main reason to give a subagent a narrow tool set rather than every available tool?
options: It is required before any MCP server can be registered with the host
It allows the subagent to run without any system prompt at all
It limits unintended actions and aids predictability
It makes the subagent's responses shorter and cheaper to generate
sampleQuestions.explanation: Least privilege applies to agents as it does to services: fewer capabilities means a smaller blast radius and more predictable behaviour.
whyWrong: There is no such precondition on registering an MCP server.
A system prompt is still needed regardless of how many tools are exposed.
Tool count is not what determines response length or cost in any direct way.

sampleQuestions.question: A tool returns 40,000 tokens of JSON on every call, and the agent degrades over a long session. What is the best first change?
options: Return a filtered summary, with detail on demand
Call the tool less often and let the agent infer the missing data
Raise the context window and keep returning the full payload each time
Move the tool to a separate MCP server with the same response shape
sampleQuestions.explanation: The problem is context consumed per call. Returning less by default, with drill-down available, fixes the cause rather than deferring it.
whyWrong: Asking the model to infer data it could retrieve trades a context problem for an accuracy problem.
A larger window delays the same failure instead of preventing it.
Relocating the tool does not change what it returns.

sampleQuestions.question: What distinguishes an MCP resource from an MCP tool?
options: A resource can only be defined by the host, never by a server
A resource is faster to access than a tool in all transports
A resource requires authentication whereas a tool never does
A resource is data to read; a tool is an action
sampleQuestions.explanation: Resources are addressable content the model can read. Tools are callable operations with side effects or computed results.
whyWrong: Servers define resources; that is their purpose.
Access speed is an implementation detail, not the defining difference.
Authentication requirements depend on the server, not on the primitive type.

sampleQuestions.question: A team wants every developer to get the same project conventions, allowed commands and context when they run Claude Code. What should they do?
options: Ask each developer to set the same preferences in their own global settings
Have one developer run all Claude Code sessions for the team
Document the conventions in the team wiki and rely on code review
Commit the configuration files to the repository
sampleQuestions.explanation: Checking configuration into the repository makes it versioned, reviewable and automatically shared with anyone who clones it.
whyWrong: Per-developer settings drift immediately and cannot be reviewed.
Funnelling work through one person is a bottleneck, not an architecture.
A wiki page is not enforced and is not loaded into the session.

sampleQuestions.question: Which is the strongest reason to prefer a hook over an instruction in a prompt for a rule that must always hold?
options: The harness runs it, so it cannot be skipped
A hook runs after the session ends, when nothing can interfere
A hook can only be configured by an organisation administrator
A hook consumes fewer tokens than the equivalent instruction
sampleQuestions.explanation: Instructions are guidance the model may weigh against other context. Hooks are deterministic code the harness runs.
whyWrong: Hooks fire around tool calls during the session, not after it.
Hooks can be configured at project level; not only centrally.
Token cost is a minor consideration next to whether the rule is guaranteed.

sampleQuestions.question: A prompt has grown to include task instructions, output format, domain glossary and twelve examples, and accuracy is falling. What should be examined first?
options: Whether the output format section should be moved to the very end
Whether the examples contradict each other
Whether the glossary should be alphabetised for easier lookup
Whether the prompt would perform better written entirely in bullet points
sampleQuestions.explanation: Contradictory examples are a common and high-impact failure in large prompts, because the model has to resolve a conflict you did not intend to create.
whyWrong: Section position matters far less than internal consistency.
Ordering a glossary has no bearing on model accuracy.
Reformatting does not resolve a substantive conflict in the content.

sampleQuestions.question: What problem does a retry with exponential backoff solve in an agent pipeline?
options: Tools that return data in an unexpected schema
Transient failures, without amplifying load
Context exhaustion during a long multi-step task
Incorrect model output caused by an ambiguous prompt
sampleQuestions.explanation: Backoff is for failures that resolve themselves, and the increasing delay avoids adding to the pressure that caused them.
whyWrong: A schema mismatch fails identically on every retry.
Context exhaustion needs a change to what is in context, not another attempt.
Retrying an ambiguous prompt reproduces the same ambiguity.

sampleQuestions.question: A multi-agent workflow must pass findings from a research subagent to a drafting subagent. What should the coordinator pass?
options: A reference to the research subagent so drafting can query it directly
A structured summary of what drafting needs
Only the final sentence of the research subagent's response
The research subagent's entire transcript, including its tool output
sampleQuestions.explanation: Passing a structured, task-relevant summary keeps the drafting agent's context clean and makes the handoff predictable.
whyWrong: Subagents do not remain available as queryable services after they report.
One sentence usually discards the substance the drafting step depends on.
A full transcript floods the next agent's context with material it does not need.

sampleQuestions.question: Which signal best indicates that a task should be decomposed into subagents rather than handled by one agent?
options: Stages differ in tool needs and success criteria
The task involves calling more than one tool
The task takes longer than a minute to complete
The task's prompt is longer than a few hundred words
sampleQuestions.explanation: Decomposition pays off when stages genuinely differ in what they need and how you judge them, because each can then be scoped and verified separately.
whyWrong: Plenty of single-agent tasks legitimately use several tools.
Duration is a weak proxy for structural complexity.
Prompt length alone says nothing about whether stages are separable.
